Eggs of the Andean cock-of-the-rock (Rupicola peruvianus) are incubated for a period of approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a value that aligns with the extended incubation durations typical of tropical passerines. Hatchlings emerge at a relatively modest mass of 23.9 grams [Wwb = 23.9 grams], reflecting the altricial condition of the newborn chicks. This initial weight at birth stands in contrast to the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown females, which reaches 225 grams [Wwi = 225 grams], while adult males are substantially larger, with a maximum adult body mass of 283 grams [Wwi = 283 grams] for males. The significant sexual size dimorphism, with males outweighing females by nearly one-quarter, is a pronounced feature of the species and is likely linked to intense male-male competition at traditional lekking arenas, where larger body size confers a distinct advantage in territorial displays and aggressive encounters.

Field observations of Rupicola peruvianus indicate that the species follows a slow-paced life history strategy, characteristic of many long-lived Neotropical birds. Reproductive output is modest: females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically raise approximately 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches each year], a low annual fecundity that is compensated by extended parental care and high juvenile survival under good conditions. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female successfully raises her first clutch, occurs at approximately 657 days [tR = approximately 657 days] when thermal conditions average 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a relatively delayed onset of breeding that underscores the energetic demands of achieving adult body size and establishing a suitable nesting territory within the dense cloud forest.

Under stable thermal conditions comparable to those measured during active metabolic periods, specifically at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developmental trajectory of juvenile cock-of-the-rocks proceeds through several well-defined milestones. Sexual maturity, marked by gonadal activation and the development of adult plumage, is attained at 129 days after hatching [tp = 129 days after hatching], a surprisingly early completion of pubertal development relative to the delayed initiation of actual breeding at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Following the onset of reproductive maturity, young birds experience a protracted subadult period during which they refine foraging skills and establish social status. Fledging, characterized by the achievement of fully coordinated flight and independent departure from the nest, occurs approximately 43 days after hatching [tx = approximately 43 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime, a duration consistent with the moderately extended nestling phase seen in o at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]ther cotingids.

Basal metabolic rate, determined through closed-system respirometry at a thermoneutral temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], yields an oxygen consumption of 196.36 milliliters per hour [JOi = 196.36 milliliters per hour], a value that reflects the relatively low resting energy expenditure typical of frugivorous birds living in stable tropical environments. This comparatively modest metabolic requirement contrasts with the high activity costs incurred during elaborate lek displays. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 10.7 years [am = approximately 10.7 years] when individuals experience ambient temperatures around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a lifespan that is among the longest documented for passerines of equivalent body mass and which aligns with the species' delayed reproduction and low annual reproductive output as part of a bet-hedging life history strategy.

The substantial maternal investment per offspring is clearly evident in the mass of a newly laid egg, approximately 27.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 27.3 grams], equivalent to over ten percent of adult female body mass and highlighting the energetic constraints shaping the species' life history evolution in the Andean cloud forest. This high initial investment precedes an extended developmental trajectory: after a relatively rapid maturation to sexual maturity at 129 days after hatching [tp = 129 days after hatching], young birds then face a prolonged subadult phase before their first successful breeding attempt, which is recorded at 657 days since birth [tR = 657 days since birth] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Such a protracted delay between physiological maturation and actual reproduction, which is unusual among small-bodied passerines, likely reflects the intense competition for display sites on leks, where only older, more experienced males successfully attract mates.
